2. Project introduction

CIARES — the Cybersecurity Incident Analysis and Response Expert System — is a Python-based rule-based Expert System. It accepts observations about a security incident, reasons over a knowledge base of 60 manually authored IF–THEN rules, derives findings, recommends a response, executes that response against an internal simulated environment, and explains every conclusion.

The project was built for a Streamlit-only assignment in which the examiner interacts with the application exclusively through its user interface. Everything described in this document is therefore visible in the running application: rule counts, conditions, activations, justifications, working-memory provenance, decisions and before/after state changes are all generated at runtime from the same engine that the automated tests exercise.

2.1 What makes CIARES an Expert System

An Expert System is not a dashboard with security labels. It must contain encoded domain expertise, a reasoning mechanism, and an explanation facility. CIARES implements the five components required by the course material:

Component CIARES implementation
Knowledge Base 60 IF–THEN rules across five cybersecurity modules
Inference Engine Forward chaining with deterministic conflict resolution
Working Memory Per-investigation facts with three-valued logic and provenance
Explanation Facility Trace explanations and per-rule justification explanations
Knowledge Acquisition Manual curation plus structural validation and registration
User Interface Seven-page Streamlit application

The system deliberately contains no trained model, no large language model and no external reasoning service. Every conclusion can be traced to a named rule, and every rule can be traced to declared conditions and an approved source. That constraint is the point of the project: transparent, auditable reasoning rather than statistical prediction.

2.2 How to read this document

Sections 3–5 state the problem, objectives, requirements and scope. Sections 6–15 explain the architecture and each engine component, with code-level detail. Section 16 lists the complete folder structure, Section 17 explains each Python file, Section 18 presents the interface evidence, Section 19 reports testing, Section 20 records deployment status, and Section 21 states limitations and conclusions. The appendices contain the full 60-rule catalogue, the condition inventory and the scenario matrix.

All screenshots in Section 18 were captured from the running application, not mocked up.

3. Problem identification

3.1 The operational problem

Security operations centres receive more alerts than analysts can investigate manually. The difficulty is not only volume. Three deeper problems make incident triage hard:

  1. Expertise is tacit. Experienced analysts combine weak signals — a failed-login count, a successful login, an unusual location — into a judgement. That reasoning is rarely written down, so it cannot be audited, taught or reproduced consistently.
  2. Evidence is incomplete. Real investigations always contain missing facts. A system that treats "not observed" as "did not happen" produces false conclusions. A system that assumes the safest case produces false negatives.
  3. Responses must be justified. Disabling an account or isolating an endpoint has operational cost. A recommendation must identify the finding that justified it, the target it applies to and why execution is safe.

Rule-based machine learning does not solve these problems by itself. A classifier may score an alert, but it typically cannot show which conditions were satisfied, which rule produced a conclusion, or why a specific response was selected. That opacity is unacceptable in an incident-response decision.

3.2 Problem statement

There is a need for a transparent Expert System that converts incomplete security observations into traceable findings and justified responses, using explicit cybersecurity knowledge rather than an opaque model, and that can demonstrate the complete reasoning chain through a single user interface.

3.3 Why an Expert System is the right tool

Incident triage is a bounded, knowledge-intensive domain. Practitioners already reason with rules of thumb ("repeated failures followed by a success are suspicious"). Those rules can be elicited, written as IF–THEN implications, validated and executed. When the rule set is explicit, the system can explain itself by construction, and a domain expert can correct a rule without retraining a model.

CIARES therefore treats the problem as symbolic knowledge representation and forward inference, not as classification.

5.2 Functional scope

In scope

  • Manual observation entry with numeric, text and tri-state boolean fields.
  • Six predefined scenarios that supply observations and entity identifiers only.
  • Forward-chaining inference over the complete rule set.
  • Finding construction with severity and supporting rule identifiers.
  • Response recommendation with phase, priority, target, executability and reason.
  • Simulated execution of 15 response actions across 8 entity types.
  • Trace, justification, working-memory and action explanations.
  • Session history with JSON export and a JSON mirror on disk.
  • Knowledge-base validation and a machine-generated condition inventory.

Out of scope

  • Real integration with operating systems, directories, firewalls or endpoint tools.
  • Authentication, multi-tenancy or role-based access control.
  • Model training, anomaly detection or natural-language processing.
  • Automatic rule learning or rule mining.
  • Concurrent multi-incident correlation within a single investigation.
  • Production-grade persistence (the JSON mirror is single-user and best effort).

5.3 Assumptions

Numeric cut-offs are CIARES project assumptions, not universal cybersecurity standards. They are grouped in config.py so that they can be inspected and changed, and they are identified as assumptions wherever they appear in the application and in this document.

Fact field Assumed threshold Measured quantity Rules using it
failed_login_attempts 10 failed login attempts AUTH-01
concurrent_sessions 3 simultaneous sessions AUTH-07
mfa_failures 5 MFA verification failures AUTH-09
outbound_traffic_mb 500 megabytes of outbound traffic NET-02
transfer_volume_mb 1000 megabytes transferred DATA-01
download_count 100 files downloaded DATA-09
connection_attempts 20 connection attempts NET-04
denied_requests 15 denied requests NET-08

The working-day assumption is 08:00–18:00. Sources are restricted to an approved list: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, MITRE ATT&CK, CISA Guidance and CIARES Project Assumption.

6. Expert System architecture

6.1 Layered design

CIARES is organised into strict layers. The user interface never contains rule logic, and the knowledge base never contains execution logic.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ app.py — seven Streamlit pages                                   │
│ Overview · New Investigation · Scenarios · Knowledge Base        │
│ Inference Trace · Response Center · History                      │
└───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                                │ run_investigation()
┌───────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐
│ engine/pipeline.py — the single investigation pipeline           │
│ observations → working memory → inference → findings → decision  │
└───┬───────────────┬────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
    │               │                │
┌───▼─────────┐ ┌───▼──────────┐ ┌───▼──────────────┐ ┌────────────┐
│ working_    │ │ inference_   │ │ decision_engine  │ │ simulation │
│ memory      │ │ engine       │ │ action library   │ │ environment│
│ facts +     │ │ forward      │ │ target + state   │ │ 15 action  │
│ provenance  │ │ chaining     │ │ validation       │ │ handlers   │
└─────────────┘ └───┬──────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────┬──────┘
                    │                                      │
             ┌──────▼────────┐                    ┌────────▼────────┐
             │ knowledge_base│                    │ explanation_    │
             │ 60 rules      │                    │ engine          │
             └───────────────┘                    └─────────────────┘

6.2 Responsibilities

Layer Responsibility Must not do
app.py Collect input, call the pipeline, render results Contain rule logic or mutate simulated state directly
engine/pipeline.py Orchestrate one investigation end to end Re-implement inference or decision rules
engine/working_memory.py Store facts, provenance, contradictions, trace Decide which rule fires
engine/inference_engine.py Evaluate rules and fire them to a fixed point Invent facts or skip conditions
engine/decision_engine.py Turn findings into validated, ordered actions Change simulated state
knowledge_base/ Define and validate cybersecurity knowledge Know about Streamlit or simulation
simulation/ Apply validated state transitions Decide whether an action is appropriate
engine/explanation_engine.py Read records and explain them Re-run inference

6.3 The single pipeline

engine/pipeline.py::run_investigation() is the only entry point used by manual investigations, scenario runs and tests. This is an architectural safeguard: there is no second code path in which a scenario could be hardcoded to produce a particular answer.

The pipeline performs six steps:

  1. Create an Investigation record and a WorkingMemory populated with observations.
  2. Run InferenceEngine to a fixed point, recording every activation.
  3. Convert activations into findings with build_findings().
  4. Create a fresh SimulatedEnvironment (fixed inventory).
  5. Ask DecisionEngine to recommend and validate response actions.
  6. Attach activations, findings, actions, trace, termination reason and environment to the investigation record.

Because the environment is created per investigation, executing an action in one scenario cannot contaminate another scenario. Because the environment is seeded with a fixed inventory, a target such as USER-999 is rejected rather than silently created.

6.4 Design constraints

Four constraints drove most implementation decisions:

  1. No hidden reasoning. A conclusion that cannot be derived from a rule is not produced.
  2. Unknown is not False. Missing evidence must never satisfy a positive condition.
  3. One reasoning path. UI, scenarios and tests use the same pipeline.
  4. Simulation only. No real system is contacted, and the UI says so on every relevant page.

7. Knowledge Base

7.1 Representation

The knowledge base is a collection of immutable Rule objects. Each rule contains declarative metadata and a tuple of Condition objects:

Rule(
    id="AUTH-01",
    name="Repeated Authentication Failure Detection",
    module="Authentication & Account Security",
    description="A sustained series of failed logins indicates credential guessing.",
    conditions=(
        Condition("failed_login_attempts", ">=", THRESHOLDS["failed_login_attempts"],
                  "failed login attempts are at or above the configured threshold"),
    ),
    conclusion_key="repeated_authentication_failures",
    conclusion_label="Repeated authentication failures",
    severity=Severity.HIGH,
    source="MITRE ATT&CK",
)

A condition is a triple (field, operator, value) plus an optional human label. It is data, not a lambda, for three reasons:

  • it can be printed exactly as authored;
  • it can be validated structurally;
  • it can be evaluated with three-valued logic and recorded in an explanation.

Supported operators are ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, in and not in.

7.2 Rules versus conditions

The assignment distinguishes rules from logical conditions. CIARES makes the distinction explicit:

  • a rule is one IF–THEN implication;
  • a condition is one comparison inside the IF part.

A three-condition rule therefore counts as one rule and three conditions. The Knowledge Base page computes both numbers from the rule objects, which prevents the condition count from drifting away from the code.

Current totals:

Metric Value
Rules 60
Logical conditions 85
Distinct fact fields referenced by conditions 80
Modules 5
Actionable rules 19

7.3 Module distribution

Module Rules Logical conditions Actionable rules
Authentication & Account Security 12 17 4
Malware & Process Security 12 18 4
Network Security 12 16 4
Data Security & Protection 12 17 3
Privilege & Security Policy 12 17 4

Each module contains exactly 12 rules. The condition count varies because some rules corroborate several indicators while others test a single fact.

7.4 Severity distribution

Severity Authored rules Findings across the six scenarios
Critical 23 25
High 24 28
Medium 13 15
Low 0 0
Total 60 68

Severity is a property of a finding, not a filter. A Critical finding never suppresses a High finding; both remain visible and both are counted on the Security Overview.

7.5 Authoring principles

  1. One conclusion per rule. A rule may not derive two facts. This keeps justification unambiguous.
  2. Conclusions are snake_case fact keys. They can be referenced by later rules, which is how chaining works.
  3. No self-supporting rules. A rule's conclusion may not also be one of its conditions. The Knowledge Acquisition module rejects this.
  4. Actionable rules declare phase and entity type. Diagnostic rules deliberately carry no action.
  5. Approved sources only. A rule must cite one of the approved references.
  6. Thresholds live in config.py. The knowledge base contains no unexplained magic numbers.
  7. Distinct, meaningful conclusions. Rules are not padding; the coverage test requires every rule to fire in at least one shipped scenario.

8. Five knowledge modules

The knowledge base is divided into five specialised modules, each with 12 rules. The division mirrors how security teams separate identity, endpoint, network, data and policy concerns.

8.1 Authentication & Account Security (AUTH-01 … AUTH-12)

Investigates credential attacks, suspicious login sequences and session misuse. Key facts include failed login attempts, successful login after failures, unusual location, disabled account access, administrator privilege, concurrent sessions, MFA failures, password changes, impossible travel and active session state.

Representative rules:

  • AUTH-01 derives repeated authentication failures when the failure count reaches the configured threshold.
  • AUTH-04 combines three independent indicators into a possible account compromise.
  • AUTH-05 detects an attempt to authenticate to a disabled account.
  • AUTH-10 detects impossible travel.
  • AUTH-12 recognises a suspicious active session.

8.2 Malware & Process Security (MAL-01 … MAL-12)

Investigates suspicious executables, process behaviour, persistence and log tampering. Facts include unapproved paths, approved-list membership, unauthorized operations, protected-file modification, digital signatures, shell spawning, persistence entries, cleared logs, known hashes and temporary-directory placement.

Representative rules:

  • MAL-01 detects execution from an unapproved directory.
  • MAL-02 fires only when a process is explicitly not on the approved list — an Unknown value cannot satisfy it.
  • MAL-07 detects shell spawning by an untrusted process.
  • MAL-08 detects persistence mechanisms.
  • MAL-12 escalates active intrusion with concealment.

8.3 Network Security (NET-01 … NET-12)

Investigates connections, destinations, ports, traffic volume, beaconing and remote access. Facts include destination authorization, port approval, remote-access authorization, inbound connections, beaconing intervals, listening services, outbound volume, connection attempts and denied requests.

Representative rules:

  • NET-01 detects access to an unauthorized destination.
  • NET-02 detects unusual outbound volume.
  • NET-07 detects command-and-control beaconing.
  • NET-10 detects an unexpected listening service.
  • NET-12 escalates an active network compromise.

8.4 Data Security & Protection (DATA-01 … DATA-12)

Investigates data movement, unauthorized access, external sharing, after-hours access, unapproved modification and deletion. Facts include transfer volume, download count, destination authorization, restricted-file access, external sharing, access hours, unapproved modification and protected-data deletion.

Representative rules:

  • DATA-01 detects an unusual data transfer.
  • DATA-03 detects unauthorized access to restricted files.
  • DATA-04 combines transfer volume and destination authorization into possible exfiltration.
  • DATA-11 chains unusual transfer and unauthorized destination into a two-stage exfiltration finding.
  • DATA-12 escalates confirmed data exfiltration.

8.5 Privilege & Security Policy (POL-01 … POL-12)

Investigates privilege escalation, unauthorized administrative operations, control tampering, separation-of-duties violations and coordinated attacks. Facts include privilege escalation, administrator grants, approval state, disabled controls, unauthorized admin operations, unapproved configuration changes, self-approval, dormant privileged accounts and restricted resource access.

Representative rules:

  • POL-01 detects privilege escalation.
  • POL-02 detects an unauthorized privilege assignment.
  • POL-05 detects a security-policy violation.
  • POL-10 detects active control tampering.
  • POL-12 is a cross-module rule: its condition possible_account_compromise is the conclusion of AUTH-04.

8.6 Cross-module chaining

Modules are not isolated. A conclusion derived in AUTH becomes a fact that a POL rule can use. SCN-005 demonstrates this explicitly: AUTH-01 through AUTH-04 derive a possible account compromise, and POL-12 then combines that fact with privilege escalation to conclude a coordinated privilege compromise. This is the strongest evidence that the rules form a knowledge base rather than five unrelated lists.

9. IF–THEN rule examples and condition inventory

9.1 Example 1 — a simple threshold rule (AUTH-01)

IF  failed_login_attempts >= 10
THEN repeated_authentication_failures = True
Severity: High

The threshold is a CIARES project assumption. It is read from config.THRESHOLDS, so changing the configuration changes the rule's behaviour without editing the rule. A count of 3 does not satisfy the condition, and the application reports that no rule fired (Figure 16).

9.2 Example 2 — evidence combination (AUTH-04)

IF  repeated_authentication_failures = True
AND suspicious_login_sequence = True
AND unusual_location_login = True
THEN possible_account_compromise = True
Severity: Critical
Response: disable_account

AUTH-04 is the clearest demonstration of AND logic. One indicator alone is insufficient: the rule fires only when three independently derived facts corroborate each other. This is evidence combination, not a list of alerts. Its conclusion is then available to POL-12.

9.3 Example 3 — the meaning of False (MAL-02)

IF  process_on_approved_list == False
THEN unapproved_process = True
Severity: High

MAL-02 fires only on an explicit False. If the fact is Unknown, the condition cannot be evaluated and the rule is ineligible. That is the operational difference between "the process is not approved" and "nobody checked whether the process is approved". A system that confused the two would generate false incidents from missing data.

9.4 Example 4 — cross-module reasoning (POL-12)

IF  privilege_escalation_detected = True
AND possible_account_compromise = True
THEN coordinated_privilege_compromise = True
Severity: Critical

The second condition is the conclusion of AUTH-04. POL-12 therefore cannot fire until the authentication module has completed its own reasoning. This is forward chaining across module boundaries.

9.5 Condition inventory

The inventory is machine-generated by validate_catalogue(). For every condition field it records how many conditions reference the field and how many distinct rules use it. The full 80-row inventory appears in Appendix B; the application renders the same table at the bottom of the Knowledge Base page (Figure 5).

The top of the inventory shows the most reused facts. For example, possible_account_compromise is referenced by two conditions in two rules, which is exactly what cross-module chaining requires.

9.6 Full catalogue

Appendix A lists all 60 rules with their IF conditions, conclusions, severity, recommended response and source. The catalogue is generated from the registered objects, so it cannot disagree with the running system. The Knowledge Base page renders the same data live (Figure 2).

10. Working Memory

10.1 Definition

Working memory is the set of facts that are true of this investigation. It is created afresh for every run and discarded when the investigation ends. The knowledge base is general and permanent; working memory is particular and temporary.

10.2 Three-valued logic

State Storage Meaning Example
True Fact(value=True) Confirmed observation or derived conclusion Unusual location detected
False Fact(value=False) Explicitly observed as absent Process is not on the approved list
Unknown key absent or Fact(value=None) Not established Login location not provided

Condition.evaluate(observed, known) returns (True | False | None, note). A rule is eligible only if every condition returns True. A single None or False makes the rule ineligible. This is the core defence against inventing incidents from missing evidence.

The Boolean fields in the UI default to Unknown, while numeric fields default to 0 and are treated as known. That asymmetry is deliberate: a zero count is a measurement; an unanswered Boolean is not.

10.3 Fact structure and provenance

Every fact records where it came from:

Fact(
    key="possible_account_compromise",
    value=True,
    source="AUTH-04",
    derived=True,
    rule_id="AUTH-04",
    supporting=(
        ("repeated_authentication_failures", True),
        ("suspicious_login_sequence", True),
        ("unusual_location_login", True),
    ),
)

Provenance is what makes the Explanation Facility possible. The working-memory page shows each derived fact, the rule that derived it and the supporting facts (Figure 9).

10.4 Contradiction handling

A fact is never silently overwritten. Working memory raises ContradictionError when:

  • an observation tries to overwrite a derived fact;
  • two observations assert different values for the same fact;
  • a rule derives a value different from an established value.

Rejecting contradictions is safer than last-write-wins. It makes inconsistent evidence visible instead of hiding it.

10.5 Trace

Working memory also records the reasoning log: observations, start, each activation, diagnosis, decision and finish. The trace is the raw material for the trace explanation and for the Markdown investigation report.

10.6 SCN-001 working memory

Derived fact Value Derived by Supporting facts
repeated_authentication_failures True AUTH-01 failed_login_attempts
suspicious_login_sequence True AUTH-02 successful_login_after_failures
unusual_location_login True AUTH-03 unusual_login_location
possible_account_compromise True AUTH-04 repeated_authentication_failures, suspicious_login_sequence, unusual_location_login

11. Forward-Chaining Inference Engine

11.1 Why forward chaining

Incident analysis is evidence-first: the analyst starts with observations and asks what they imply. Forward chaining matches that direction. Backward chaining would start from a hypothesis ("the account is compromised") and search for support, which is less suitable when the incident type is unknown and multiple conclusions may coexist.

11.2 Algorithm

The engine uses a one-rule-per-cycle loop:

fired = {}
while cycles < max_cycles:
    eligible = []
    for rule in rules:
        evaluations = evaluate(rule, memory)
        if not all_satisfied(evaluations): continue
        key = activation_key(rule, entities, evaluations)
        if key in fired: continue
        eligible.append((rule, evaluations, key))

    if eligible is empty:
        terminated_reason = "fixed point"
        break

    sort eligible by (severity desc, priority asc, rule id)
    rule, evaluations, key = eligible[0]
    memory.infer(rule.conclusion, True, rule, support)
    fired.add(key)
    record_activation(...)

Three decisions matter:

  1. Fire one rule, then re-evaluate. Firing every eligible rule in one batch is faster but records an order that did not actually drive the reasoning. CIARES prioritises a truthful trace.
  2. Deterministic conflict resolution. Highest severity, then author priority, then rule ID. Ties never depend on dictionary iteration order.
  3. Explicit termination. If no eligible activation remains, the engine reports a fixed point. A cycle cap (max(100, 5 × rule count)) is a safety guard, not the normal exit.

11.3 Activation tracking

An activation key is:

rule_id :: sorted(entity_id=value) :: condition_field=observed_value

This prevents the same rule from firing repeatedly on identical evidence. It also allows the same rule to fire once per entity set, which is the foundation for future multi-account analysis. If a supporting value changes, the key changes and the rule may legitimately fire again.

11.4 Termination

Working memory is monotonic: facts are added, never retracted. The set of derivable facts is finite, and each activation key can fire at most once. The loop therefore reaches a fixed point. In all six shipped scenarios the reported reason is fixed point: no further eligible rules.

11.5 SCN-001 trace

# Rule Name Conclusion Severity New fact
1 AUTH-01 Repeated Authentication Failure Detection Repeated authentication failures High Yes
2 AUTH-02 Successful Login After Failures Suspicious login sequence High Yes
3 AUTH-03 Unusual Login Location Unusual-location login Medium Yes
4 AUTH-04 Possible Account Compromise Possible account compromise Critical Yes

The order is the real reasoning order, recorded as the engine ran. AUTH-04 could not fire until AUTH-01, AUTH-02 and AUTH-03 had inserted their conclusions into working memory.

11.6 Complexity and scale

With 60 rules and a bounded number of facts, the engine is trivially fast in practice. Each cycle evaluates at most 60 rules, and the number of cycles is bounded by the number of distinct activations. The design favours explainability and determinism over asymptotic cleverness. That is appropriate for an Expert System whose rule base is authored by humans.

12. Decision and Response Engine

12.1 Diagnosis versus decision

The inference engine answers "what is happening?"; the decision engine answers "what should we do about it?". They are separate for a reason: a diagnostic rule can report a problem without inventing a response, and an actionable rule can recommend a response only when it has produced a finding.

A Finding is a diagnosis with severity, module, supporting rule IDs and an optional recommended action. A ResponseAction is a concrete instruction with phase, priority, target type, target ID, executability, status and reason.

12.2 Action library

Action key Label Phase Priority Target Required state Purpose
isolate_endpoint Isolate affected endpoint Containment 1 endpoint status = Online Remove the endpoint from the simulated network to stop spread.
disable_account Disable affected account Containment 1 account status = Active, Locked Prevent any further authentication with the affected credential.
restrict_transfer Restrict suspicious data transfer Containment 1 transfer status = Active Stop the identified transfer before more data leaves.
revoke_session Revoke suspicious session Containment 2 session status = Active Terminate the active session associated with the finding.
restrict_connection Restrict suspicious connection Containment 2 connection status = Open Rate-limit or close the connection under investigation.
block_destination Block unauthorized destination Containment 2 destination status = Reachable Deny all traffic to the unapproved destination.
isolate_process Isolate suspicious process Containment 2 process status = Running Freeze the process while evidence is collected.
lock_account Lock affected account Containment 3 account status = Active Lock the credential pending verification with the account owner.
terminate_process Terminate suspicious process Eradication 3 process status = Isolated, Running Stop the malicious process after containment.
quarantine_file Quarantine suspicious file Eradication 4 file status = Present Move the executable to quarantine so it cannot run again.
apply_data_access_restriction Apply data-access restriction Containment 4 account data_access = Unrestricted Restrict the account to approved data sets only.
revoke_permissions Revoke unauthorized permissions Recovery 5 account permissions = Approved, Elevated Withdraw the privileges that were not approved.
restore_permissions Restore approved permissions Recovery 5 account permissions = Elevated, Revoked Return the account to the approved permission baseline.
restore_account Restore approved account status Recovery 6 account status = Disabled, Locked Re-enable the account once containment is complete and verified.
escalate_to_analyst Escalate to security administrator Escalation 7 incident status = any Refer the investigation to a human owner.

Fifteen action keys are declared once and shared by the rules, the decision engine and the simulation dispatcher. A test asserts that the decision library and the implemented handlers are exactly the same set, so a rule cannot recommend an action that has no simulator.

12.3 Decision procedure

  1. Keep only findings that carry a recommended_action.
  2. Sort by severity, then derivation order.
  3. Resolve the target from the investigation's entity map (account_id, session_id, …).
  4. Validate the target:
    • an identifier must be present;
    • the entity must exist in the simulated environment;
    • the entity must be in a state where the action makes sense.
  5. Collapse duplicate (action, target) pairs into one action, merging the reasons.
  6. Suppress recovery actions when containment already applies to the same target.
  7. Sort by phase (Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Escalation), then priority, then action key; assign ACT-001-style identifiers.

Validation failures do not hide the action. The action is shown with Executable: No and a human-readable Blocked reason, which is both safer and more informative than dropping it.

12.4 Target validation example

SCN-001 with account_id = USER-101 produces one executable containment action: disable the account. The same reasoning with account_id = USER-999 produces exactly the same finding, but the action is blocked because USER-999 does not exist in the simulated inventory (Figures 17–18). The difference proves that the decision layer validates rather than hardcodes.

12.5 Conflict handling

Two kinds of conflict are handled explicitly:

  • Inference conflicts. Multiple rules may derive different findings from the same evidence. All findings are kept; severity orders presentation but never deletes a finding.
  • Response conflicts. If a containment action targets an entity, a recovery action on the same entity is marked Skipped with a reason. Restoring access while containment is in effect would be contradictory. SCN-005 demonstrates this: 3 actions are proposed, 2 are executable, and 1 recovery action is skipped.

12.6 SCN-001 findings and actions

Finding Severity Module Rules Response
Possible account compromise Critical Authentication & Account Security AUTH-04 disable_account
Repeated authentication failures High Authentication & Account Security AUTH-01 —
Suspicious login sequence High Authentication & Account Security AUTH-02 —
Unusual-location login Medium Authentication & Account Security AUTH-03 —

The response is deliberately modest: one finding is actionable and one action is proposed. The other three findings are diagnostic. The system reports the full diagnosis without inventing a response for every line.

13. Simulated Environment

13.1 Purpose

CIARES must demonstrate response execution without touching a real account, process, host or network. The simulation layer provides a small in-memory world whose state can be changed and inspected.

13.2 Entities and states

Entity type Default state States used by actions
account Active Active, Disabled, Locked
account.permissions Approved Approved, Revoked, Elevated
account.data_access Unrestricted Unrestricted, Restricted
session Active Active, Revoked
process Running Running, Isolated, Terminated
file Present Present, Quarantined
transfer Active Active, Restricted
destination Reachable Reachable, Blocked
endpoint Online Online, Isolated
connection Open Open, Restricted

The seeded inventory contains two accounts (USER-101, USER-202), two sessions (SESSION-204, SESSION-311) and one each of process, file, transfer, destination, endpoint and connection. This is enough to demonstrate every action while keeping the world understandable.

13.3 Guarded transitions

SimulatedEnvironment.transition() accepts an allowed_from set. A transition is rejected if the entity does not exist, if no target was supplied, or if the current state is not in allowed_from. Rejections return a reason instead of raising, so the UI can display exactly why an action failed.

Examples:

  • disabling an already disabled account is rejected;
  • terminating a process that is not Running or Isolated is rejected;
  • acting on USER-999 is rejected because the entity does not exist.

13.4 Execution dispatch

simulation.execute(environment, action) is the only execution entry point. It:

  1. looks up the handler for the action key;
  2. refuses to run if the decision engine marked the action non-executable;
  3. calls the handler, which performs a guarded transition;
  4. stores an ExecutionResult on the action and sets its status to Executed or Rejected.

The decision engine never mutates state, and the simulation layer never decides whether an action is appropriate. Each layer has one job.

13.5 A deliberate design fix

An earlier implementation provisioned entities named in an investigation on demand. That made USER-999 executable: the act of naming it created it. The pipeline now uses only the fixed inventory. A regression test asserts that an unknown target is blocked at the pipeline level, not merely at the UI level. This is a good example of a safety property that emerged from testing rather than from the original design.

14. Explanation Facility

14.1 Two explanations

The Explanation Facility produces the two explanation types used in the course material:

  • a trace explanation — what fired, in what order, and what it concluded;
  • a justification explanation — for one activation, every condition with its expected value, observed value and satisfaction status.

It also explains actions: why the action was selected, whether the target check passed, what happened on execution and the before/after state.

14.2 Reading records, not re-reasoning

ExplanationEngine never re-runs inference. It reads the activation records, condition evaluations, trace entries and execution results that the engine already produced. That is important: an explanation generated by a second reasoning pass could disagree with the first. Here the explanation is a view of the same evidence.

14.3 Trace output

The trace includes:

  • the ordered activation table;
  • the reasoning log with observation, start, activation, diagnosis, decision and finish events;
  • the termination reason.

14.4 Justification output

Condition Field Operator Expected Observed Status
repeated authentication failures were derived repeated_authentication_failures == True True Satisfied
a login succeeded after repeated failures suspicious_login_sequence == True True Satisfied
the login came from an unusual location unusual_location_login == True True Satisfied

Each condition shows the field, operator, expected value, observed value and status. The closing statement explains that all conditions were satisfied and the conclusion was inserted into working memory.

14.5 Export

The same records generate a Markdown investigation report containing observations, findings, the activation trace, actions and limitations. This makes the explanation portable and suitable for a report appendix.

15. Knowledge Acquisition

15.1 Manual, curated knowledge

CIARES does not learn from data. Knowledge is elicited from approved cybersecurity references, written as explicit rules and validated before registration. This is a deliberate choice: manual curation keeps every rule inspectable and keeps the system's behaviour attributable.

15.2 Validation checks

validate_rule() enforces:

Check Failure mode
ID matches (AUTH|MAL|NET|DATA|POL)-NN error
ID is unique in the catalogue error
Name and description present error
At least one condition error
Conclusion present and not one of its own conditions error
Severity is a Severity value error
Source is approved error
Actionable rule has a snake_case action key error
Actionable rule declares a phase and a valid entity type error

validate_catalogue() additionally counts rules, conditions and distinct fact fields, builds the condition inventory, and emits warnings if a future edit drops below 60 rules or 50 conditions. KnowledgeAcquisition.register() refuses invalid rules outright.

15.3 Where validation is visible

The Knowledge Base page runs validation on every render. A green banner reports that the catalogue is valid; a red banner would list every error. The sidebar repeats the rule and condition counts, so a broken catalogue is visible from every page.

15.4 Adding a rule

The documented extension procedure is:

  1. add the rule to the relevant module tuple;
  2. reuse or add an action in ACTION_LIBRARY and a handler in simulation/;
  3. run python -m pytest;
  4. add the rule to a scenario so the coverage test can prove it is reachable;
  5. update docs/rule_catalogue.md.

The coverage requirement is intentional: a rule that can never fire is not knowledge, it is decoration.

15.5 Sources

Each rule cites one approved source. The source is displayed in the Knowledge Base and in the justification, so a reader can see whether a rule is grounded in NIST guidance, MITRE ATT&CK, CISA guidance or an explicit project assumption. Numeric thresholds are always identified as assumptions, never as standards.

17. Explanation of each Python file

17.1 Root-level files

app.py — the Streamlit entry point. It configures the page, injects the CSS theme, renders the sidebar and dispatches to seven page functions: page_overview, page_new_investigation, page_scenarios, page_knowledge_base, page_trace, page_response_center and page_history. It owns session state (active investigation, history list) and calls the pipeline. It contains no rule logic.

config.py — central configuration. Contains the application identity, data paths, threshold assumptions, approved sources and the working-day assumption. Keeping thresholds here is what allows the report to say honestly that they are configurable project assumptions.

requirements.txt — runtime dependencies: Streamlit, pandas and pytest. Documentation build dependencies are intentionally not part of the application requirements.

17.2 engine/

models.py — pure data structures: Severity, Phase, Condition, Rule, Fact, ConditionEvaluation, RuleActivation, Finding, ResponseAction, ExecutionResult and Investigation. It also implements three-valued condition evaluation and boolean-safe equality (so True does not equal 1). No business logic lives here.

working_memory.py — per-investigation fact store. Adds observations, inserts derived facts with provenance, rejects contradictions, records the trace and exposes observations, derived facts and provenance queries.

inference_engine.py — the forward-chaining loop. Evaluates every rule, computes activation keys, sorts eligible rules deterministically, fires one rule per cycle, inserts its conclusion and repeats to a fixed point.

decision_engine.py — the action library and decision procedure. Resolves targets, validates existence and state, deduplicates actions, suppresses recovery after containment, orders actions by phase and priority and assigns action identifiers.

pipeline.py — the single investigation pipeline. Builds findings from activations, creates the simulated environment, invokes the decision engine and assembles the Investigation record. Also contains severity aggregation for the dashboard.

explanation_engine.py — converts records into trace rows, justification tables, action explanations and a Markdown report. It never re-reasons.

17.3 knowledge_base/

authentication.py — AUTH-01 to AUTH-12. Twelve rules covering failures, suspicious sequences, locations, disabled accounts, off-hours admin logins, concurrent sessions, password changes, MFA brute force, impossible travel, confirmed compromise and suspicious sessions.

malware.py — MAL-01 to MAL-12. Twelve rules covering unapproved paths, approved-list membership, unauthorized operations, protected files, signatures, shell spawning, persistence, log tampering, unknown hashes, temporary directories and coordinated malware activity.

network.py — NET-01 to NET-12. Twelve rules covering unauthorized destinations, traffic volume, ports, repeated connections, remote access, inbound connections, beaconing, denied requests, listening services, data transfer and active compromise.

data_security.py — DATA-01 to DATA-12. Twelve rules covering transfer volume, downloads, destination authorization, restricted files, external sharing, after-hours access, modification, deletion, bulk access, exfiltration and integrity violations.

security_policy.py — POL-01 to POL-12. Twelve rules covering privilege escalation, unauthorized assignment, control changes, suspicious privileged activity, policy violations, unauthorized admin operations, configuration changes, separation of duties, dormant privileged accounts, control tampering, insider threat and coordinated compromise.

rule_registry.py — concatenates the five module tuples into ALL_RULES, exposes RULES_BY_MODULE, MODULES and module_summary(). The inference engine imports ALL_RULES rather than importing each module separately.

knowledge_acquisition.py — validation and registration. Checks structure, uniqueness, severity, source, conclusion and action consistency; counts conditions and distinct fact fields; builds the condition inventory.

17.4 simulation/

environment.py — the simulated world. Declares entity types, default states and the seeded inventory; implements existence checks, snapshots and guarded state transitions; provides apply_change() for action modules.

account_actions.py — disable, lock, restore, revoke session and permission recovery handlers.

network_actions.py — restrict connection, block destination and isolate endpoint handlers.

process_actions.py — isolate process, terminate process and quarantine file handlers.

data_policy_actions.py — restrict transfer, data-access restriction and permission revocation handlers.

__init__.py — aggregates all handlers into ALL_ACTIONS, exposes available_actions() and implements execute(), including refusal of non-executable actions.

17.5 scenarios/

sample_scenarios.py — six scenario definitions. Each supplies observations, entity IDs and expected finding keys for verification. No scenario supplies a diagnosis or a response.

17.6 tests/

conftest.py — adds the project root to sys.path so tests run without installation.

test_rules.py — 17 tests: threshold behaviour, Unknown versus False, corroboration, condition semantics, catalogue integrity.

test_inference.py — 10 tests: chaining order, fixed point, no re-fire, activation keys, provenance, contradiction handling.

test_decisions.py — 11 tests: target validation, state validation, duplicates, containment/recovery conflict, ordering, action-library consistency.

test_simulation.py — 11 tests: successful transitions, rejected transitions, missing targets, blocked actions, snapshots.

test_scenarios.py — 30 tests: six end-to-end scenarios, JSON-serialisable records, no preloaded diagnoses, missing-evidence behaviour.

test_coverage.py — 13 tests: exactly 60 rules and 12 per module, at least 50 conditions, every rule reachable, every actionable rule produces a response, every executable action succeeds, phase ordering, explanation completeness.

17.7 Documentation and scripts

README.md explains installation, architecture and usage. docs/rule_catalogue.md documents all 60 rules. docs/rule_sources.md maps rules to references. docs/technical_design.md explains the implementation. docs/demo_guide.md is the UI-only viva script. docs/screenshots/ stores the evidence images. scripts/build_pdf.py and scripts/print_pdf.cjs reproduce this document, and scripts/capture_screenshots.mjs captures the interface evidence.

19. Testing and results

19.1 Strategy

The test suite verifies both components and behaviour. Rule tests check individual conditions; engine tests check chaining and termination; decision tests check safety; simulation tests check state transitions; scenario tests check complete investigations; and the coverage test prevents the knowledge base from being padded with unreachable rules.

Test file Tests What it verifies
tests/test_coverage.py 13 60 rules, 12 per module, ≥50 conditions, every rule reachable
tests/test_decisions.py 11 Target/state validation, duplicates, containment/recovery, ordering
tests/test_inference.py 10 Chaining order, fixed point, no re-fire, provenance, contradictions
tests/test_rules.py 17 Thresholds, Unknown vs False, corroboration, condition semantics
tests/test_scenarios.py 30 Six end-to-end scenarios, serialisation, no preloaded diagnoses
tests/test_simulation.py 11 Successful and rejected transitions, blocked actions, snapshots
Total 92 —

19.2 Coverage guards

test_coverage.py enforces the assignment's quantitative claims:

  • exactly 60 rules and exactly 12 per module;
  • at least 50 logical conditions;
  • every registered rule fires in at least one shipped scenario;
  • every actionable rule produces a response action;
  • every executable action succeeds against the simulated environment;
  • actions are ordered by response phase;
  • every activation has a complete justification.

This is the answer to the obvious examiner question: "How do you know the 60 rules are real and not padding?" If a rule cannot fire, the test suite fails. All 60 are currently reachable.

20.2 Deployment notes

  • History uses data/investigations.json when the filesystem is writable and degrades to session-only history when it is not.
  • The simulated environment is per-investigation and per-session; no state is shared between users.
  • No secrets, credentials or external services are required.

21. Limitations and conclusion

21.1 Limitations

  1. Simulated responses only. Every action changes an in-memory object. This is a safety feature and a scope boundary, not a claim of real remediation.
  2. Manual knowledge acquisition. Rules are authored and validated by hand. The system does not learn, and it cannot discover new attack patterns.
  3. Single-focus investigations. The UI supplies one identifier per entity type per run. The activation key already supports multiple entities, so multi-entity correlation is an extension rather than a redesign.
  4. Monotonic inference. Facts are added and never retracted. There is no non-monotonic reasoning or belief revision.
  5. Numeric observations are always known. Only Boolean facts are tri-state, so a numeric zero is treated as a measurement rather than as missing data.
  6. Thresholds are assumptions. The cut-offs are configurable CIARES project assumptions, not audited industry standards.
  7. Local history. Persistence is a best-effort JSON mirror with no authentication or multi-user isolation.
  8. Static rule coverage. The six scenarios exercise all 60 rules, but they cannot represent every combination of evidence.

21.2 Future work

  • Multi-entity investigations with correlation across accounts, hosts and sessions.
  • A rule editor backed by the Knowledge Acquisition module.
  • Confidence factors or fuzzy thresholds for graded evidence.
  • Integration adapters for real telemetry, behind an explicit safety boundary.
  • Richer response planning, including rollback and verification steps.
  • Exportable audit reports with signatures.

21.3 Conclusion

CIARES demonstrates that a cybersecurity incident-response Expert System can be built with transparent symbolic reasoning rather than an opaque model. It contains 60 manually authored rules and 85 logical conditions across five modules, reasons with three-valued logic, chains rules across module boundaries, validates response targets, executes actions against a simulated environment and explains every conclusion at condition level.

The project meets the functional requirements: a Streamlit-only interface, a real Python inference engine, a knowledge base above the required size, a working-memory model, decision-making with simulated execution, an explanation facility, knowledge acquisition and a 92-test verification suite. Its boundaries are stated honestly: responses are simulated, knowledge is curated manually, and thresholds are project assumptions.

That combination — working system, visible evidence and acknowledged limits — is the strongest position from which to demonstrate and defend the project in a viva.

POL-02 Unauthorized Privilege Assignment administrator privileges were granted AND the permission change was not approved unauthorized_privilege_assignment Critical revoke_permissions NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3
POL-03 Unauthorized Security-Control Change a security control was disabled unauthorized_security_control_change Critical — MITRE ATT&CK
POL-04 Suspicious Privileged Activity an unauthorized privilege assignment was derived AND an unauthorized administrative operation occurred suspicious_privileged_activity Critical revoke_permissions NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3
POL-05 Security Policy Violation a restricted resource was accessed without permission security_policy_violation High — MITRE ATT&CK
POL-06 Unauthorized Administrative Operation an administrative operation was unauthorized unauthorized_admin_operation High — MITRE ATT&CK
POL-07 Unauthorized Configuration Change security configuration changed without approval unauthorized_configuration_change Medium — MITRE ATT&CK
POL-08 Separation-of-Duties Violation the change was approved by its own requester separation_of_duties_violation High — NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
POL-09 Dormant Privileged Account Risk a dormant account still holds privileges dormant_privileged_account_risk Medium — CISA Guidance
POL-10 Active Control Tampering a security control was disabled without authorization AND security configuration changed without approval active_control_tampering Critical — MITRE ATT&CK
POL-11 Insider Threat Suspected a dormant privileged account risk was derived AND suspicious privileged activity was derived insider_threat_suspected Critical escalate_to_analyst CISA Guidance
POL-12 Coordinated Privilege Compromise privilege escalation was derived AND the authentication module derived a possible account compromise coordinated_privilege_compromise Critical disable_account NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3

Appendix D — Glossary

Term Meaning
Activation One rule firing against the current facts
Activation key Rule ID + entity IDs + supporting values; prevents duplicate firing
Antecedent The IF part of a rule
Consequent The THEN part of a rule
Condition One comparison inside a rule antecedent
Finding A diagnosis derived from a rule conclusion
Fixed point The state in which no further rule is eligible
Forward chaining Data-driven inference from facts to conclusions
Justification Condition-level explanation of why one rule fired
Knowledge base The permanent collection of rules
Monotonic Facts are only added, never retracted
Response action A concrete, validated instruction derived from a finding
Three-valued logic True, False and Unknown, where Unknown is not False
Trace The ordered record of observations, activations and decisions
Working memory The facts of the current investigation
